Paul Ganguly

Please note that “aortic arches” are different from “arch of the aorta”
Pharyngeal arches (just get the concept)-six of them (four visible)-responsible for the formation of head and neck of the embryo-each supplied by a separate nerve and artery

[Visual transcription, authored after inspection]
Hand-drawn embryo: aortic arch arteries between aortic sac and dorsal aorta.

The main concept
When pharyngeal arches form during the fourth and fifth weeks of development, each arch receives its own cranial nerve and its own artery
These arteries, the aortic arches, arise from the aortic sac-the distal part of truncus arteriosus
The total number of arteries present in aortic arches is 6 on either side of the embryo (Total=12)
Immediately after that some disappear and the area is supplied by next arteries in the line

[Visual transcription, authored after inspection]
Paired dorsal aortae and numbered arch channels I, II, III, IV, VI connect to the ventral outflow; diagram is a developmental schematic, not a simultaneous persistent six-pair adult arrangement.
Now get a concept of aortic arch that forms through the migration of neural crest. The arches join dorsal aorta
Aortic arches and the initial heart tube. Observe aortic sac at the distal part of truncus arteriosus

Although six pairs of pharyngeal arches usually develop, they are not present at the same time
By the time the sixth pair of pharyngeal artery is developed, the first two pairs disappeared
The fifth arch either never forms or forms incompletely and then regress
The arrangement of the arteries will explain why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve lower in the left side
Also look at carefully for the 7
th
 intersegmental artery for the formation of left subclavian artery

[Visual transcription, authored after inspection]
Diagram labels external and internal carotid, common carotid, aortic arch, right subclavian, right/left pulmonary artery, ductus arteriosus and seventh intersegmental arteries.

[Visual transcription, authored after inspection]
Third arch: common carotid and first part internal carotid; remainder internal carotid from cranial dorsal aorta. External carotid sprouts from third arch region. Fourth: left part aortic arch, right proximal right subclavian. Fifth absent or regresses. Sixth proximal pulmonary arteries; distal right disappears; distal left persists as ductus arteriosus.

[Visual transcription, authored after inspection]
Remodeling diagram: internal/external carotids, carotid duct, right dorsal aorta obliteration, brachiocephalic, seventh intersegmental, pulmonary artery, ductus arteriosus and aortic arch.

Observe the position of the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves. The left is below the ductus arteriosus. The right goes up and stays below right subclavian artery because of the disappearance of right 6
th

Table: first maxillary; second hyoid/stapedial; third common carotid and first internal carotid; left fourth arch between left common carotid and left subclavian; right fourth proximal right subclavian; left sixth pulmonary artery/ductus; right sixth pulmonary artery. Footnotes: external carotid sprouts from third; rest internal carotid dorsal aorta; right aortic sac horn forms brachiocephalic, left proximal arch; seventh intersegmental makes entire left and distal right subclavian.

Intercostal space, 
Diaphragm
CVP 112
Olena Bolgova, MD, PhD
Professor of Gross Anatomy
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this lecture students should be able to describe:

Intercostal space, intercostal muscles

Diaphragm, Phrenic nerve

Clinical cases:
Intercostal nerve block
Flail chest  “stove-in chest”
Paralysis of half of the diaphragm
Diaphragmatic rupture
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Intercostal spaces
Intercostal blood vessels and 
nerves:

run between the internal 
intercostal and 
innermost intercostal 
muscles in the costal 
groove 

arranged from superior to 
inferior as vein, artery, 
nerve

Most vulnerable
structures – intercostal 
nerve and posterior 
intercostal artery 
because ribs do not cover 
them.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Intercostal nerve block

Local anesthesia of an 
intercostal space is produced 
by injecting a local anesthetic 
agent around the intercostal 
nerves between the 
paravertebral line and the 
area of required anesthesia. 

Because any particular area 
of skin usually receives 
innervation from two 
adjacent nerves, 
considerable overlapping of 
contiguous dermatomes 
occurs. 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Intercostal muscles

External intercostal muscle 

extends from the rib tubercle 
posteriorly to the costochondral 
junction anteriorly where the 
muscle fibers are replaced by the 
external intercostal membrane

Internal intercostal muscle

extends from the sternum 
anteriorly to the rib angle 
posteriorly where the internal 
intercostal membrane replaces the 
muscle fibers

Innermost intercostal muscle

similar to the internal intercostal 
muscle (deep portion) - separated 
by intercostal VAN
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Flail chest (“stove-in chest”)

It occurs when a large 
anterior or lateral chest wall 
segment moves freely due to 
multiple rib fractures
(paradoxical respiration).

Loose segment of the wall 
moves inward on inspiration
and outward on expiration.

Flail chest is an extremely 
painful injury that impairs 
ventilation, affecting blood 
oxygenation and causing 
respiratory failure.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

DIAPHRAGM

Parts:

sternal part – from xiphoid process

costal part – from lower 6 ribs and 
their costal cartilages

vertebral part – from the bodies 
and IV discs of lumbar vertebrae by 
means of vertical columns or crura
and from the arcuate ligaments

Central Tendon – where diaphragm 
inserts

clover-leaf shaped to which the 
muscle fibers of the diaphragm insert

superior surface partially fused to 
inferior surface of the fibrous 
pericardium
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Movements of the diaphragm
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Openings of the diaphragm

Caval (T8): transmits 
the IVC and the 
terminal branches of 
the right phrenic
nerve

Esophageal (T10): 
transmits the 
esophagus, right and 
left vagus nerves, 
esophageal branches of 
the left gastric 
vessels

Aortic (T12) transmits 
the descending aorta, 
thoracic duct, 
azygos vein
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Nerve supply & function of the 
diaphragm

Motor: phrenic nerve 
(C3-C5) ONLY

Sensory:

phrenic nerve - central 
portion

lower 6 intercostal nerves -
peripheral portion

Diaphragm is the muscle 
of inspiration: contraction 
pulls down the central 
tendon increased vertical 
diameter of the thorax 
decreased intrathoracic
pressure expansion of 
the lungs 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Phrenic nerve 

It arises from the anterior 
branches of C3-C5 nerves
and lies in front of the 
anterior scalene muscle.

Phrenic nerve runs anterior
to the root of the lung, 
whereas the vagus nerve runs 
posterior to the root of the 
lung.

It innervates the fibrous 
pericardium, the 
mediastinal and 
diaphragmatic pleurae
(sensory innervation), and 
the diaphragm for motor
and its central tendon for 
sensory.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Paralysis of half of the 
diaphragm

It may result from 
injury or operative 
division of the 
phrenic nerve of 
same side

It can be detected 
radiologically. 

Paradoxical 
movement: dome of 
diaphragm of injured 
side pushed superiorly 
by abdominal viscera 
during inspiration 
instead of descending
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Diaphragmatic ruptures

Diaphragmatic injuries are relatively rare 
and result from either blunt trauma or
penetrating trauma.

Presently, 80-90% of blunt 
diaphragmatic ruptures result from 
motor vehicle crashes.

The majority (80-90%) of blunt 
diaphragmatic ruptures have occurred on 
the left side.

Blunt trauma typically produces large 
radial tears measuring 5-15 cm, most 
often at the posterolateral aspect of 
the diaphragm.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Main muscles of respiration

Muscles of inspiration:
Diaphragm
External intercostal
Serratus posterior superior 
muscle 

Muscles of expiration:
Internal & innermost 
intercostal
Serratus posterior inferior 
muscle  

In quiet breathing, expiration 
results from passive elastic 
recoil of the lungs and rib cage
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Movements of 
the thoracic wall

The vertical dimension (height) of the 
central part of the thoracic cavity increases 
during inspiration as a contraction of the 
diaphragm causes it to descend, 
compressing the abdominal viscera.

The AP dimension of the thorax 
increases considerably when the 
intercostal muscles contract: movement 
of the ribs at the costovertebral joints 
around an axis passing through the necks 
of the ribs causes the anterior ends of the 
ribs to rise - the pump-handle 
movement

The transverse dimension of the thorax 
also increases slightly when the 
intercostal muscles contract, raising the 
middle of the ribs - the bucket-handle 
movement
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Accessory muscles of 
respiration

Muscles of forced inspiration
- elevate sternum and/or fix 
upper ribs

Srternocleidomastoid

Scalenes (anterior, middle, 
and posterior)

Pectoralis major

Serratus anterior

Muscles of forced expiration
- depress the lower ribs 

Rectus abdominis

External abdominal oblique

Internal abdominal oblique

Transversus abdominis
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Lungs Anatomy
CVP 112
Olena Bolgova, MD, PhD
Professor of Gross Anatomy
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this lecture students should be able to describe:

Anatomy of right and left bronchi

Anatomy of lungs

Clinical cases:
Aspiration of foreign bodies 
Bronchopulmonary segments 
Bronchogenic carcinoma (Pancoast tumor)
Pneumonia
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

The respiratory system 
includes the lungs and 
respiratory ways that link 
the sites of gas exchange with 
the external environment.  

There is also a ventilation 
mechanism, consisting of the 
thoracic cage, intercostal 
muscles, diaphragm, and 
elastic and collagen 
components of the lungs, that 
is important in the movement 
of air through the conducting 
and respiratory parts of the 
lungs.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

TRACHEA

It is a thin-walled tube about 
10-13 cm long and 2.5 cm in 
diameter

It consists of 16-20 C-shaped 
rings of hyaline cartilage 
embedded in its fibroelastic wall 
and which serve to keep the 
tracheal lumen patent

It extends from the lower border 
of the cricoid cartilage (C6) in 
the neck to the level of the 
sternal angle (IV disc T4/T5) in 
the superior mediastinum, where 
it divides into the right and left 
primary (main) bronchi
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Carina

It is a ridge separating the 
openings of the main bronchi 
at their junction with the 
trachea

The carina: may be 
examined with a 
bronchoscope and may be 
distorted, widened 
posteriorly, and immobile
in the presence of 
bronchogenic carcinoma. 

The mucous membrane over 
the carina is one of the most 
sensitive areas of the 
tracheobronchial tree and is 
associated with the cough 
reflex
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Right primary bronchus

It is shorter (1 cm), wider, 
and more vertically
disposed than the left 
primary bronchus

Upper lobar (secondary) 
bronchus (Eparterial
bronchus) – given off 
before entering the hilum
of the right lung, all other 
bronchi are hyparterial
bronchi.

Middle and inferior lobar 
bronchi – given off after 
entering hilum
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Left primary bronchus

It is longer (2 cm), 
narrower, and more 
horizontal than the right 
primary bronchus

It passes to the left inferior
to the arch of the aorta and 
anterior to the esophagus

Upper and inferior lobar 
bronchi – given off after
entering the hilum of the left 
lung
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Aspiration of foreign bodies

Inhalation of FBs (pins, parts 
of teeth, screws, nuts, bolts, 
toys) into the lower 
respiratory tract is common, 
especially in children

More likely to enter the 
right primary bronchus 
and pass into the middle or 
lower lobe bronchi

If the vertical position of the 
body, the foreign body 
usually falls into the 
posterior basal segment 
of the right inferior lobe.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

LUNGS (Pulmones)

The right lung is divided into 3 
lobes (superior, middle, inferior) 
separated by two fissures, the 
oblique and horizontal fissures. 
The horizontal fissure separates the 
superior from the middle lobe and 
the oblique fissure separates the 
middle from the inferior lobe.

The left lung is divided into two 
lobes (superior, and inferior) 
separated by an oblique fissure. 
The lingula of the upper lobe of 
the left lung corresponds to the 
middle lobe of the right lung.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Parts of the lungs

Apex

Base - sits on the 
diaphragm

Surfaces:
Costal - corresponds 
to the thoracic wall
Mediastinal - faced 
the mediastinum
Diaphragmatic –
related to diaphragm

Anterior border: cardiac 
notch – left lung only
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Left lung

It is divided by the oblique 
fissure into 2 lobes: upper 
and lower

Hilum – depression located 
at about the center of the 
mediastinal surface -

Root of the Left lung ABV: 
1 pulmonary Artery,
1 main Bronchus, 
2 pulmonary Veins

Mediastinal surface:
Aortic arch
Left subclavian 
artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Right lung

slightly larger than the left

divided by the oblique and 
horizontal fissures into 3 
lobes: upper, middle, and 
lower

Right lung: BAV 
1 main Bronchus , 
1 pulmonary Artery,
2 pulmonary Veins

Mediastinal surfice:
Azygos vein
SVC
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Bronchopulmonary segments

It is the largest subdivision of a lung 
lobe: pyramidal in shape (apex 
directed toward lung root and base 
at the pleural surface)

Separated from adjacent
segments by surrounded by 
connective tissue septa

Supplied independently by a 
segmental (tertiary) bronchus
and a tertiary branch of the 
pulmonary artery

Drained by intersegmental parts of 
the pulmonary veins that lie in the 
connective tissue between and 
drain adjacent segments

Diseased segment can be resected 
surgically
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Bronchogenic carcinoma

Arises in the mucosa of the 
large bronchi

Produces a persistent, 
productive cough or 
hemoptysis

Early metastasis to thoracic
(bronchomediatinal) lymph 
nodes

Hematogenous spread to the 
brain, bones, lungs, and 
suprarenal glands

A tumor at the apex of the lung 
(Pancoast tumor) may result 
in Thoracic Outlet Syndrome 
and Horner Syndrome
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Bronchogenic carcinoma
(Pancoast tumor) may lead to:
1. Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS)

It can cause pressure on the lower 
trunk of the brachial plexus C8-T1 and 
subclavian artery by a cervical rib or
pancoast tumor. It results in pain
down the medial side of the forearm 
and hand and atrophy of the intrinsic 
hand muscles)
2. Horner syndrome:
1.
ptosis - drooping of the eyelid due to 
paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle
2.
miosis - constriction of the pupil due 
to paralysis of the dilator pupillae 
muscle
3.
hemianhydrosis - loss of sweating on 
one side of the face
1

may lead to:
3. Superior vena cava 
syndrome, which causes 
dilation of the head and 
neck veins, facial 
swelling, and cyanosis
4. Dysphagia as a result of 
esophageal obstruction
5. Hoarseness as a result 
of recurrent laryngeal 
nerve involvement
6. Paralysis of the 
diaphragm as a result 
of phrenic nerve 
involvement

Blood supply and lymphatic 
drainage of the lungs
Arteries:

bronchial arteries – from 
the thoracic aorta supply 
the structures comprising 
the root of the  lung, 
supporting tissues of the 
lung, and the visceral pleura
Veins:

bronchial veins drainage 
to azygos system of veins
Lymphatic Drainage:

bronchomediastinal
lymph nodes and trunks 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pneumonia

Pneumonia is an inflammation of 
the lung, caused by an infection or 
chemical injury to the lungs. 

Three common causes are 
bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

Symptoms: cough, chest pain, 
fever, and difficulty in breathing. 

Chest x-rays: areas of opacity
(seen as white) of the lung 
parenchyma and enlargement of 
bronchomediastinal lymph nodes
(mediastinal widening).

Lung
The lungs are a pair of spongy, air-
filled organs located on both sides of
the chest.
They are covered by a thin tissue
layer called the pleura.

The trachea divides into two branches
forming the right and left main (primary)
bronchi, which enter the hilum through
the posterior side of each lung.
Each primary bronchus divides into the
lobar (secondary) bronchi. The right
primary bronchus divides into 3 lobar
bronchi and the left into 2 lobar
bronchial branches, with each branch
supplying one lobe.
In the right lung, the lobar (secondary)
bronchi
give
rise
to
10
segmental
(tertiary) bronchi; the lobar bronchi of
the left lung give rise to 8 segmental
bronchi, with each branch supplying one
bronchopulmonary segment.
Each
bronchopulmonary
segment
is
subdivided into pulmonary lobules; each
lobule is supplied by a bronchiole.

Bronchioles
The wall of bronchioles is composed of:
1. Mucosa:
Epithelium (next slide)

2. Muscularis: A relatively thick layer of smooth

3. Adventitia: Connective tissue, attached to the

I. INTRODUCTION
Oxygen (O2) is essential for our survival. We need it to generate most of the energy required for our
cells to function. We call the process of supplying O2 to our cells, respiration. The complex
physiological system in charge of transporting O2 from the atmosphere to the cells is called the
respiratory system.
Although transporting O2 is the primary duty of our respiratory system, it has other vital functions.
One is transporting another gas, carbon dioxide (CO2), from the cells where it is produced to the
environment. CO2 is a byproduct of metabolism which is toxic at high levels; therefore, eliminating it
efficiently is essential.
As shown in the figure, a series of transport systems is involved in transportation of gases between
atmosphere and cells of the body. O2 is transported by a convective process called ventilation from
atmosphere into the lung. It passes the lung alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion and then is
transported to systemic capillaries by circulation.
Finally, O2 leaving capillaries reaches the
mitochondria of the cells by the process of diffusion. In mitochondrion O2 is metabolized for
production of ATP. CO2 generated by this metabolism will be then transported through the same
mechanisms but in the opposite direction from the cell to the atmosphere. O2 partial pressure drops
at each step of its transport to the tissue from an ambient value of 150 mm Hg (at sea level) to a
value close to 1-2 mm Hg in the mitochondria. The causes for this reduction in PO2 will be described
in the course of upcoming lectures. CO2 partial pressure decreases from 45 mmHg in the cells to
zero outside the body. Consider that all these transport systems are in series, so that if O2 transport
is interrupted at a certain location, there will be no transport down stream of that location.

II. STRUCTURE OF THE RESPIRATORY TRACT
The primary functions of the respiratory tract are to transport gases between the environment and the body and to provide an exchange
area between the air and blood. The distance between the environment and the blood flowing in the lungs is fairly long, about 1/3 of a
meter. Long distant transport and the exchange of substances are also the primary functions of the circulatory system. It is not surprising
then that both the circulatory system and the respiratory tract share some very basic structural features. In the respiratory tract, gases are
transported through tubes that branch into progressively smaller and smaller tubes, similar to blood flowing through the circulatory
system. The smallest structures in the respiratory tract, like those in the circulatory system, are the most numerous, providing an
extensive area for the exchange of material. Because of these structural similarities, the physical forces that move material through these
systems act in similar ways.
A. Upper Respiratory Tract (not shown): The first structure of the upper respiratory tract is the nose. When we inhale with our mouths
closed, air enters the respiratory tract by flowing through the nostrils and then into the nasal cavity. Air then flows into the pharynx, and
from there into the larynx. The structures from the nose to the larynx constitute the upper respiratory tract. The lining of the upper
respiratory tract receives a large amount of blood flow, and it is coated with mucous. The blood not only serves its usual functions, but it
also warms and moistens the mucous, which in turn, warms and moistens the air before it flows into the lower respiratory tract. Mucous
also entraps inhaled particulate matter such as dust. These features "condition" the air so that it does not cool or irritate the deeper and
more delicate respiratory tissues.
B. Lower Respiratory Tract: The lower respiratory tract is structured like a tree trunk with roots spreading out beneath it (Figure 2). The
trunk is the trachea, a short tube about 2 -2.5 cm in diameter that extends from the larynx and splits into two slightly smaller tubes called
main bronchi. One main bronchus goes to the right lung, the other to the left lung. The main bronchi split into smaller bronchi, like tree
roots, which then divide into still smaller bronchi. The bronchi contain cartilage, making them fairly rigid, and smooth muscle which can
alter diameter. After the bronchi divide about 15 times, the air tubes are ~1 mm in diameter and are called bronchioles. Unlike the
bronchi, bronchioles have no cartilage, although they do contain a considerable amount of smooth muscle. The bronchioles, like the
bronchi, split into even smaller tubes. After about a dozen divisions, very small sacs (≈0.5 mm in diameter) called alveoli appear on the
sides and at the ends of the smallest bronchioles. The alveoli are extremely important because they are the exchange sites where gases
move between the air in the lungs and the blood. Consequently, this deep region of lung is called the gas exchange region (respiratory
zone). In the gas exchange region, there are no air currents and gases move only by diffusion. The other parts of the respiratory tract
(the bronchioles, bronchi, trachea, and upper respiratory tract) are called the conducting airways because air moves through them by
bulk flow, not diffusion.

C. Dead Space (conducting zone) and Gas Exchange Space (respiratory zone):
Airways branch into 23 generations. The first 16 generations constitute the conducting
airways. No exchange of gases (O2 and CO2) between the gaseous phase and blood takes
place within these airways, and therefore they are collectively called anatomical dead
space.
Alveoli begin to appear in the wall at the end of the last 7 divisions, in which gas
exchange between the air and the blood takes place. This region is called alveolar- or gas
exchange region. Some areas of the alveolar region may not participate in gas exchange if
they are collapsed or not perfused with blood. Thus, these areas behave functionally like
dead space. Since there is no gas exchange in these areas, this volume is
added to the
anatomical dead space, and both are referred to jointly as physiological dead space.
Remember that physiological dead space can only be greater than or equal to anatomical
dead space. The lung volume at the end of a normal expiration in adults is about 3 liters.
Only 5 % of this volume, e. g. 150 ml, is the dead space volume (VD), while the rest of the
volume resides in alveolar space. Total lung volume ranges from a maximum of 7 L and a
minimum of 1.5 L. Interestingly these changes occur only in alveolar volume, whereas VD
remains virtually the same. The volume of our breath (tidal volume; VT) during normal
breathing is about 500 ml, from which 150 ml (~1/3) remains in dead space (VD) and 2/3
(~350 ml) reaches alveolar space (VA).
The alveolar surface area available for gas exchange is 1 m2/Kg body mass or about 70 - 90
m2, with a very thin alveolar capillary barrier of 1 – 1.5 µm. Both a large surface and a thin
gas-blood barrier are essential for an effective gas exchange.

I. Lung Volumes
Lung volume is simply defined as the gas volume in the lung. This volume is not
constant and changes with breathing. In general, one part of the lung volume can
be mobilized by breathing (modifiable lung volume) and another part cannot (resting
volume). After a maximal expiration the lung is not empty and contains still
approximately 1.5 L air. This volume at the end of a maximal exhalation is called the
Residual Volume.
With normal exhalation we do not empty the lung to this low
volume and approximately 3 L air remain in the lung. 1.5 L of it is the residual
volume and the other 1.5 L is called Expiratory reserve volume. During normal
breathing we continually inhale and exhale about 0.5 L. It means that the lung
volume changes from the end of a normal exhalation to the end of a normal
inhalation by approximately 0.5 L and this volume is called the Tidal Volume. At
the end of a normal inhalation, we can further inhale 2.5 L by a maximal inspiratory
effort, and this volume is called Inspiratory reserve volume.

A. Spirometry
A spirometer is a device used to measure the modifiable volume of the lung. A simple
spirometer is a gas container with a variable volume that can be recorded on a registration
paper. If connected to a patient through a tube, changes in lung volume of the patient can
be recorded as changes in spirometer volume. As lung volume increases (inspiration), the
spirometer volume decreases and vice versa. The following three lung volumes can be
measured by the spirometer:
1.
Tidal Volume (VT): volume of air moved into and out of lung during normal
quiet breathing (0.5 L).
2.
Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV): After a quiet inspiration, the additional volume of
air inspired with maximum effort ( 2.5 L).
3.
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV): After a quiet expiration, the additional volume of
air expired with maximum effort (1.5 L).
Even after expiration with maximum effort the lung is not empty. About 1.5 L air remains in
the lung, which can not be exhaled and therefore can not be measured with a spirometer.
This volume is called rest volume or residual volume (RV). One method to measure this
volume (helium diluting method) is described in the next slide.

I. Compliance of the respiratory system
The lung and chest wall are two distensible bodies, whose compliances are essential for the
respiratory function. We will discuss some essential mechanical properties of an elastic
balloon, before elaborating on compliances of lung and chest wall.
A. Compliance of a balloon
As shown in the figure, a balloon can be inflated in two ways. Either a volume dV is injected
into the balloon increasing inside pressure (Pi), or the volume dV is removed from the inside
of non compressible box decreasing outside pressure of the balloon (Po). In both cases
expansion of the balloon with volume dV is associated with a positive transmural pressure
difference (Pi – Po) independent of whether inside pressure is increased or outside pressure
is decreased. This transmural pressure difference (Ptm) is the distending pressure for the
balloon and inflates the balloon by volume dV. If the experiment is repeated with different
volumes, and all volumes are plotted against their corresponding Ptm values, we obtain the
relationship between volume and distending pressure of the balloon, and the curve displaying
this relationship is called Volume/Ptm curve (see above figure). The slope of this curve
represents compliance, which is defined as changes in volume (dV) divided by changes in
transmural pressure difference (dPtm). If a small change in distending pressure, Ptm, causes
a large change in volume, the balloon is obviously more compliant. Please consider that the
slope of this V/Ptm curve and thus compliance of the balloon is not constant and depends on
the volume of the balloon. The higher the balloon volume the lower is its compliance.

B. Compliance of the lungs, chest wall, and respiratory system
The lung and chest wall (including diaphragm) both behave functionally like two elastic balloons. Now one is
placed in the other like a tube in a tire. The lung and chest wall considered together as one elastic body is called
the respiratory system. If we want to determine individual compliances for the lung, chest wall and respiratory
system, we have to record their volumes at the corresponding transmural pressure differences. An increase in
lung volume by dV would cause the same increase in the volume of the chest cavity. Therefore, changes in the
volume for all three lung, chest wall and respiratory system are identical, but the Ptm for these structures are
different:
Ptm for the lung: Inside the lung we have alveolar pressure (PA) and at the outer surface of the lung resides
pleura with pleural pressure (PPl). Thus, transmural pressure for the lung is (PA - PPl).
Ptm for the chest wall: Pleural pressure constitutes also the inner chest wall pressure, whereas pressure at
outer chest surface is barometric. Thus, thorax transmural pressure difference is (PPl - PB).
Ptm for the respiratory system: For the respiratory system (the lung and chest considered together as one
elastic body) the distending pressure will be alveolar minus barometric pressure (PA – PB).
Please make sure that barometric pressure is set to zero by convention.
Compliance for lung (CL), chest wall (CCW), and respiratory system (CRS) can then be derived from dV and the
corresponding transmural pressure differences as these are shown in the above figure. The lung and chest wall
are in series so that reciprocal values of their compliances added to the reciprocal value of compliance for
respiratory system: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW .

A summary slide of previous three slides:
To understand more about the mechanical properties of the respiratory system, we need to illustrate the volume/distending pressure curves
of the respiratory system and of its components, the lungs and chest wall. To do so the following necessary parameters have to be
measured:
1. Lung volumes with a spirometer.
2. Pleural pressure (PPl) with a pressure manometer advanced into the esophagus (last third) with a balloon prior to the tip of measuring
device. Inflation of the balloon interrupts direct communication of esophagus interior with the mouth. In this case esophageal pressure is
equal to dorsal mediastinal pressure, which in turn equals pleural pressure.
3. Alveolar pressure (PA) with a pressure manometer connected to airways. This pressure equals PA, only in steady state with no gas flow
and by open epiglottis.
Volume/distending pressure curves can now be illustrated by plotting of lung volumes against PPL for the chest wall, against (PA – PPL) for
lung and against PA for the respiratory system. These curves are shown in the figure. First, we want to analyze the curve for the respiratory
system (solid curve). Remember the slope of this curve represents compliance of the respiratory system (CRS). The greatest slope and thus
highest CRS is obtained at volumes close to FRC (resting volume of the respiratory system). As volume increases largely above FRC or
decreases largely below FRC, the slope of the curve and consequently CRS decreases. Therefore, we experience a more compliant
respiratory system during normal quite breathing, whereas maximal inspiration or expiration is exerted against a less compliant respiratory
system.
The lung curve (dotted curve) indicates that the lung has a high compliance in the range of normal breathing and at low lung
volumes, whereas its compliance significantly decreases at high lung volumes (lowest slope).
This is a mechanism to prevent the lung
against a possible damaging large distention. On the other hand, the lowest compliance of the chest wall (see slope of dashed curve) is
observed at residual volume restricting further expiration. From mechanical point of view, we can say that maximal inspiration is restricted by
the lung, while chest wall restricts maximal expiration. The lung and chest wall are in series. Therefore, reciprocal values of their
compliances add to the reciprocal value of the compliance of respiratory system: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW
Resting volumes: Resting volume of a hollow elastic body is achieved at transmural pressure of zero. Being above or below of resting
volume, the body would recoil towards its resting volume. Recoiling force depends certainly on compliance of the body and is inversely
related to it. The higher compliance the lower would be the recoiling force. Resting volume of the lung is far below residual volume at 300 ml
(also called minimal lung volume), which can never be achieved in intact respiratory system. On the other hand, resting volume of the chest
wall is at 60% of TLC (see the figure). Therefore, at FRC lung is recoiling inwards, while thorax is recoiling outwards. These antagonistic
recoiling forces of lung and thorax are equal at FRC Thus all passive forces acting on respiratory system are on balance at FRC.
Consequently, FRC constitutes resting volume of the respiratory system.
Another consequence of these opposing recoiling forces is a
negative PPL at FRC, because pleural space holding lung and thorax together is pulled in opposite directions by the recoil of these two at
FRC.
When taking a breath, we move the respiratory system away from its resting volume (FRC). Therefore, active muscle force is required to compensate for the
recoiling force of RS. During quite expiration RS is moving toward FRC releasing energy, which overcomes airway resistance. Thus, expiration is normally
passive. Expiration below FRC requires again energy and is an active process.

D. Changes in compliance with lung disease
Many chronic respiratory diseases are associated with changes in lung compliance.
A significant loss of lung tissue is observed with chronic obstructive lung disease
(emphysema). It causes the lung to be more compliant and thus the volume–
pressure curve is shifted to the left. Increased compliance strengthens the
obstruction particularly during expiration and makes breathing even more difficult.
Lung fibrosis, on the other hand decreases compliance (shifting the curve to the
right) and reduces the expansion capability of the lung.
More muscle work is
needed during inspiration to increase lung volume.
Remember that the ideal compliance is the normal lung compliance. A compliance
change in either direction is not beneficial.

E. Factors determining lung compliance
At least four factors are involved in determining the lung compliance:
1. Elastic material of the lung tissue. The number and geometrical organization of
elastin and collagen fibers are responsible for nearly half of the elastic recoil in
normal lungs. Surface tension (see below) accounts for the other half of the
recoiling force.

independent of surrounding alveoli at a constant lung volume. Whenever one
alveolus collapses or reduces its volume, the surrounding alveoli will become
expanded. Increasing the volume of neighboring alveoli causes their compliance to
decrease resisting further expansion. In fact, this alveolar interaction prevents a
collapse of alveoli and affects the lung compliance.

3. Effect of Surface tension on Compliance

Surface tension
In this experiment, the lung is gradually filled either with water (left curve) or with air 
(right curve) and the filling volume (lung volume) is ploted against filling pressure 
(transmural pressure). It is obvious that filling the lung with water occures much
easier than when filling the lung with air. It means that for filling the lung with air a 
much high pressure is needed compared to filling it with water. In the case of water 
filling no surface tension is produced, because water and lung tissue (composed of 
70 % water) constitute the same medium and do not build an interface between the 
two different media. In the case of air filling, air in contact with lung tissue (mostly 
water) builds an interface between air and tissue, which in turn produces suface 
tension. The property of surface tension is to reduce the surface area to a minimum 
for a given volume. It means that surface tension resists an expansion of the 
surface and therefore, a higher pressure is needed to overcome this force for 
inflation of the lung. In other words, surface tension acts to decrease lung 
compliance.

3. Surface tension: Surface tension occurs at the air-liquid interface. Molecules in
the bulk of a solution will be pulled equally in all directions by the intermolecular
force of neighboring molecules. Thus, the net force acting on them is zero. At the
air-fluid interface, however, the force pulling molecules upward is missing.
Therefore, the resultant force on surface molecules is downward directed. Some
surface molecule then dive into the bulk fluid leaving the others on the surface
under tension, which is called surface tension (ST).
The effect of surface tension is to keep the air-fluid surface as small as possible (for
a given volume). Therefore, rain drops (fluid in air) or air bubbles (air in fluid) are
spherical, because a round body has the smallest surface area for a given volume.

pressure (due to Laplace) would empty into larger alveoli with lower inside pressure.

4. Surfactant: Surfactant is a surface-active agent molecule that has both a
hydrophilic head (strongly attracted to water) and a hydrophobic tail (strongly
repelled by water). The hydrophilic heads of surfactant points toward (and interacts
with) the most superficial water molecules, whereas the hydrophobic tails point
toward the air (see the figure). These hydrophobic tails exert a counter force to
hydrophilic heads and pull the surfactant upward toward the air. This prevents
surfactant at the air-surfactant interface from diving into the bulk water. Therefore,
surfactant molecules themselves produce very little or no surface tension. By
replacing water molecules from the surface in contact with the air, they abolish the
surface tension of the replaced water molecules. As a result, the air-water interface
becomes smaller and causes a much smaller surface tension (produced by the
remaining water molecules at the interface).
Surfactant is a mixture of lipids and proteins. Lipids make up approximately 90% of
surfactant and are responsible for the surface-active properties. Proteins account
for the remaining 10% of pulmonary surfactant. Plasma albumin and Ig A make up
about half of the protein, and four apoproteins (SP-A, -B, -C and -D) make up the
rest. SP-A may be important for exerting feed back control that limits surfactant
secretion. SP-B and SP-C are membrane proteins and responsible for the entering
rate of surfactant at air-water interface that spreads as a surface film.

shift to the right.
This is particularly a problem for infants born prematurely, since synthesis and
secretion of surfactant are quite low until immediately before birth, when a surge
in maternal glucocorticoid levels triggers these processes. Therefore, infants
with low surfactant levels (IRDS) must expend tremendous muscle work to
expand their lungs.
2. Surfactant minimizes fluid accumulation in alveoli. In normal lungs, Starling
forces favor fluid movement from the alveolar space into the interstitium,
keeping the alveoli dry. In the absence of surfactant, increased surface tension

Now we assume both alveoli are inflated unequally, because the lower alveolus has a higher

(1) The total surface area of the two alveoli is less than if they had inflated equally, impairing

(2) Based on volume, the ventilation of the upper alveolus would be greater than that of lower
alveolus, and unevenness of ventilation impairs effective gas exchange.

other hand, the slower expanding alveolus having a higher surfactant density at interface can
further expand more easily. Thus, the surfactant effect results in a more equal expansion of
the two alveoli. Remember that the inequality of surfactant density (being larger in smaller

F. Changes in pressure and volume during breathing
A cycle of breathing is associated with changes in pleural and alveolar pressures, as well
as changes in lung volume and air flow. Variations of these parameters during inspiration
and expiration are displayed in the figure.
At the end of expiration (no flow), PA is zero with PPL = -6 cm H2O, resulting in a Ptm = +6
cm H2O. This Ptm is the required lung distending pressure for the volume FRC.
Contraction of the diaphragm during inspiration causes further decreases in PPl (from -6 to -
9 cm H2O), that exerts two effects:

flow means inspiration).
(2) It causes Ptm to increase for further distension of the lung covering a higher volume
FRC + VT (= 0.5 l).

4. The chest wall is elastic like the lung but normally (at

I. Airway Resistance
As you learned earlier, a parallel system of branching airways (including all bronchi and
bronchioles) that connects the atmosphere with the alveolar space is called conducting
airways. During inspiration, the air flows through the airways from the atmosphere into the
alveoli and moves in the opposite direction during expiration. Air volume passing through
the airways in a unit of time is called air flow (V). Driving force producing air flow is the
pressure difference between both ends of the airways. For expiration, this pressure
difference would be: Alveolar pressure (PA) minus pressure at airway opening (Pao).
Airway resistance (Raw) can be then obtained due to Hagen-Poiseuille law as shown
above.
Therefore, PA, Pao and airflow should be measured to use for the calculation of airway
resistance. Pao is zero (atmospheric pressure), and airway flow can easily be measured
with a pneumo-tachometer. A direct PA measurement is nearly impossible, because
alveolar space is not easily accessible for applying noninvasive methods. However,
techniques have been developed for indirect measurement of PA such as interrupter
method or the whole-body plethysmography.
Changes in airway resistance induced by natural stimuli occur by changes in airway radius.
The principal changes are achieved either actively by alterations in the contraction of the
airway smooth muscle cells, or passively by changes in transmural pressure of airways.
Recall from geometry that cross sectional area of a tube is equal to πr2, so changes in
radius have magnified effects.

A. Distribution of airway resistance
Airways branch like a tree in 23 generations, so the total number of airways goes from one
to 223 or 8,388,608.
The radius of individual bronchi becomes smaller from generation 1 to 23, but the total
diameter of all bronchi within one generation decreases only in the first 4 generations. This
leads to the increase of total resistance in the early four dividing generations.
Thereafter total airway diameter increases rapidly from generation to generation toward
peripheral airways. As a result, total airway resistance exhibits a sharp decrease toward
peripheral airways. Only 20% of the total airway resistance is then localized in the
peripheral airways beyond dividing generation 7, although very narrow airways are residing
in this region of the lung (diameter below 2 mm). Consequently, the major site of airway
resistance is in upper airways, prior to division 7 (80%).
A disadvantage of this resistance distribution is called “silent lung disease”; i.e., even large
peripheral lung tumors do not constrict the large airway diameter of this region to a level
that could produce obstructive symptoms or to be detected by measurement of Raw. On the
other hand, small obstruction in upper airways produces a significant change in Raw.

As a lung region becomes relatively hyperventilated and its PCO2 decreases, airway

Assessing pulmonary function
Most of respiratory diseases are associated with changes in Raw or CRS. Measuring Raw and CRW is
not so easy and cannot be performed in every physicians office. What matters for a physician is to
be able to evaluate and observe changes in above parameters, but knowing their absolute values is
not essential. Therefore, several functional tests (easy to apply) have been developed to serve this
goal. These tests are introduced below:
I. Forced Expiratory Vital Capacity
To measure forced vital capacity the patient is asked to take a maximum breath in, hold it for a
second, then exhale as hard and fast as he/she can.
The most important data derived from this
maneuver are:
1.
Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1): It is the volume of air that is forcibly exhaled from
the lungs in the first second of a forced expiratory maneuver.
2.
Forced Vital Capacity (FVC): After a maximal inspiration, the volume of air that is forcibly and
maximally exhaled until no more can be expired.
3. Ratio of FEV1/FVC which is normally 0.8 (80%).
4.
Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR): The maximum flow rate achieved during the forced vital
capacity maneuver beginning after full inspiration and starting and ending with maximal
expiration.
These spirometry variables will be discussed later to help understand normal lung physiology and to
diagnose specific lung pathology.

Q2. Explanation (D): Compliance is defined as dV/dP. Inhaling 2 L means that 
lung volume increased by 2L, therefore, dV = 2L. Now pressure before 
inhalation of dV was 5 cm H2O and thereafter 10 cm H2O; therefore, dP = 10 –

Q3. Explanation (D): Total ventilation is equal to alveolar ventilation + dead 
space ventilation. It means (FR x VT) = (FR x VA) + (FR x VD). Therefore 
changes in FR affects all three ventilations proportionately, but changes in VT 
affects VA, but not VD (VD is virtually constant). In this question Total 
ventilation is the same by all choices. A decrease in FR decreases both alveolar 
and dead space ventilation, but increases in VT would only increase alveolar 
ventilation, but not dead space ventilation. Therefore a combination of highest 
VT and lowest FR for a given total ventilation would result in the highest 
alveolar ventilation and lowest dead space ventilation.  
Q4. Explanation (E): Physiologic dead space = anatomic dead space + those 
alveolar regions that have no gas exchange. Therefore, physiologic dead space 
is greater than anatomic dead space if some alveoli are ventilated but not 
perfused with blood. On the other hand, if all alveoli take part in gas exchange, 
physiologic dead space equals anatomic dead space. However, physiologic dead 
space will never be smaller than anatomic dead space.

Q6. Explanation (E): Radial traction of the airway means that the airway is 
pulling outwards by the recoil force of the lung, increasing airway transmural 
pressure difference that in turn dilates the airway. Therefore, a loss of this 
force produces a narrowing of the airway and results in a decreased FEV1.
